DC Water’s Blue Plains Advanced Wastewater Treatment Plant (BP AWWTP) is the largest plant of its kind, worldwide. On an average day, BP AWWTP treats close to 300 million gallons of wastewater and is capable of treating over a billion gallons a day at peak flow. It handles inflows from the District of Columbia, Montgomery and Prince George’s Counties in Maryland, and Fairfax and Loudoun counties in Virginia. BP AWWTP employs HR-CS for secondary treatment following chemically enhanced primary treatment (CEPT). It precedes the tertiary treatment where nitrogen removal is performed. In addition to the primary effluent, the HR-CS system receives two return flows that are hypothesized to influence performance: (i) the solids processing building (SPB) line produced during the thickening and dewatering processes, and (ii) waste nitrification sludge (WNS) from the downstream tertiary nitrification process. At BP AWWTP, it was observed that bio- augmenting the A-stage HR-CS process with WNS may positively influence settleability (i.e., ability of solids to settle out of suspension and form a sludge layer at the bottom) and overall process performance, whereas supernatant return flow from the SPB may negatively influence process stability (Van Winckel et al. 2019). Here, it is worth noting that the high-rate systems operate at very short solids retention times where wastage rates are high. At Blue Blains, wastage rate is at the maximum of the solids processing capacity. Accordingly, there is no room to perform conventional return flow management and manipulate wastage and return rates. Carbon diversion relies on biosorption of slowly biodegradable carbon to biomass and subsequent solids-liquid separation via settling in a clarifier, with carbon-laden waste biomass routed to digestion. The system is operated in a highly dynamic manner where high mass and volumetric loading rates are applied. As a result, a key challenge in this and other A-stage processes is sludge settleability and the associated maintenance of effluent quality, particularly effluent suspended solids (ESS) (AlSayed et al. 2023). An A-stage process in wastewater treatment, also known as the adsorption stage, is a biologically enhanced primary treatment that removes organic matter by flocculation and sorption to sludge.
